title: The flat carton photo
scenario:
You are the designer for an oat-milk brand. The client wants a web banner: the carton on the right, and an empty area on the left for a headline that your team will add in the design tool.

Your first prompt gave a flat, dull picture with a busy background. The exhibit shows the prompt, the result and the client's notes.
exhibit:
First prompt
  "A carton of oat milk, no clutter, beautiful, high quality"

What came back
  Straight-on carton, grey flat light, cluttered shelf behind it,
  carton centred in the frame, square image.

Client notes
  - Warm morning feel, like a kitchen
  - Carton on the right, empty space on the left for a headline
  - Landscape banner shape
  - Headline will be added by us, not drawn by the model

questions.prompt: Which rewrite fixes the most problems in the first prompt?

options.text: "A product photograph of a white oat-milk carton on a pale oak table, bottom-right of frame, soft warm window light from the left, empty wall on the left, 3:2."
options.explanation: Right. It names the subject, setting, light, camera and format, and it asks for empty space on the left. This follows Google's photo and negative-space templates.

options.text: "An amazing, stunning, ultra-beautiful carton of oat milk on a kitchen table, best quality, perfect, 8k, masterpiece, trending, award-winning photo, very sharp."
options.explanation: These words add praise, not information. The model still has to guess the light, the angle and the setting.

options.text: "A carton of oat milk, no clutter, no shelf, no grey light, no centred carton, no flat look, no square shape, no busy background, no dull colours."
options.explanation: This is a list of things to avoid. Google's tip is to describe what you want, not what you don't want.

options.text: "A carton of oat milk on a kitchen table, with the words 'Wake up gently' written large across the empty area on the left side of the frame."
options.explanation: The client said the team adds the headline. Asking the model to draw words risks wrong text and takes space you need to control.

questions.prompt: The first prompt said "no clutter" and the shelf was still busy. What is the better way to write that wish?

options.text: Write it in capital letters and add three exclamation marks: "NO CLUTTER!!!".
options.explanation: Capital letters don't change what the docs recommend. Describing the scene you want works better than shouting a ban.

options.text: Describe the scene you want: "a clean table with only the carton".
options.explanation: Right. Google's tip is a semantic negative prompt: describe the intended scene in positive words, like "an empty, deserted street" instead of "no cars".

options.text: Repeat "no clutter" five times at the start and end of the prompt.
options.explanation: Repeating the same ban adds no new detail about the picture you want.

options.text: Remove the setting from the prompt so there is nothing to clutter.
options.explanation: Without a setting the model picks one for you. Naming the setting is how you control it.

questions.prompt: You have 6 different prompt ideas and a deadline. What is a sensible way to use OpenAI's quality setting?

options.text: Render all 6 at the highest quality, so none of them look rough and none need a redo.
options.explanation: OpenAI's docs say to use low quality for quick drafts, and to compare higher settings for final assets. The highest setting for all 6 spends time and money on ideas you may drop.

options.text: Run all 6 as low-quality drafts, then render the best at higher quality and compare.
options.explanation: Right. This is the advice in OpenAI's docs: low for quick drafts, then compare higher settings for final assets to balance detail, latency and cost.

options.text: Never use low quality. It makes the prompt less accurate and wastes the first render.
options.explanation: The docs don't say that. They recommend low quality for drafts.

options.text: Pick one prompt at random and render it once at the lowest quality, then send it.
options.explanation: That skips the comparison. Drafts are cheap so you can compare several ideas before choosing.

questions.prompt: The client later asks for a version where the carton says "Oat. Simply." inside the picture. What is the safest plan?

options.text: Give the exact words in the prompt and send the first result, since the exact words were already in the prompt.
options.explanation: OpenAI's docs say its model can still struggle with precise text placement and clarity. Never skip the check.

options.text: Give the exact words, read every letter of the result, and set the text in your design tool if it is wrong.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI lists text placement as a limitation, and Google advises generating the text first. Proof-reading costs little, and a design tool gives you exact control.

options.text: Ask the model to draw the words in bold capitals so they come out clearer and easier to read.
options.explanation: Bold capitals don't fix text clarity. You still have to read every letter.

options.text: Skip the check, because the client will notice errors in review and can ask for a fix.
options.explanation: A wrong word that reaches the client is your mistake. Check it before you send.
